transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-29
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Alex (CTO, Nova), Renee (SRE Lead), Samir (Platform Eng), Lena (Security Lead)

AUTO SUMMARY: Intake on incident readiness and backstop routing. Discussed acceptable degraded modes, jurisdictional failover limits, telemetry, and pilot criteria.

00:00:03 Maya (AE): All right everyone thanks for making time. Quick round of intros then we'll jump into the failure modes you want covered and what acceptance looks like.
00:00:12 Alex (CTO): Hi -- main thing is we want automatic backstops. Last time latency spiked, engineers had to manually throttle flows which is not sustainable.
00:00:20 Diego (SE): Understood. We'll map out the failure modes: per-region latency spikes, cache cold-start, model OOMs, and upstream vendor failures. Which should we prioritize?
00:00:28 Renee (SRE): Priorities: 1) deterministic behavior on region latency >500ms, 2) predictable degradation rather than cascading failures, 3) forensic logs for the incident window.
00:00:38 Priya (SE): Redwood supports route-level policies: prefer local region, then try a quantized local variant, then remote full model. You can also do reserved warm-secondaries.
00:00:48 Samir (Platform): Quantized variant = lower quality. PMs will need to sign off on when that can be used.
00:00:54 Diego: Yep, it's an explicit policy. Typical config: local full -> local Q8 -> regional full -> external fallback. Each step has thresholds and canary windows.
00:01:05 Alex: Cache: we saw double latency on cold cache. Do you do cache priming during failover?
00:01:11 Priya: We have KV cache plus explicit prefix priming. You can earmark a hot set to remain primed during failover windows; costs go up but tail latency improves. We can show numbers.
00:01:22 Lena (Security): Jurisdiction question: if we fail to a different region, does data move across legal boundaries?
00:01:27 Maya: We can pin failover to within a jurisdiction. If you need strict residency, Dedicated or Private with VPC is recommended so we never cross boundaries.
00:01:38 Renee: Audit logs are critical. We need immutable per-request traces during the incident.
00:01:44 Priya: Console exposes per-request traces and an activity log. For Dedicated/Private we integrate with your SIEM and support customer-managed KMS. We'll attach SOC2 and security artifacts.
00:01:55 Diego: One question: do you want global SLA wording or region-by-region?
00:02:00 Alex: Product team thinks global availability; legal will push for region clauses.
00:02:06 Maya: For Dedicated we can define region SLOs and an overall availability target. Hosted customers see published performance profiles; enterprise terms cover multi-region failover behavior.
00:02:16 Samir: Cost: full active-active across 3 regions is very expensive. Our traffic split is roughly 70% NA, 20% EU, 10% APAC. We might prefer active-passive.
00:02:26 Diego: Common approach is hot-primary + warm-secondary/reserved capacity. Warm-secondaries reduce cost but have a warmup. Active-passive with fast priming often hits 90-95% of the benefit.
00:02:36 Renee: We cannot have partial routing surprises. Failovers must be atomic per route unless we intentionally ramp.
00:02:41 Priya: Routing policies can be atomic or staged. You can set thresholds for error counts or latency windows. There's also a staged canary (e.g., 5% for 1 minute then 25%).
00:02:53 Alex: Preventing cascade is key. Our previous secondary overloaded. Do you have built-in circuit breakers?
00:02:58 Diego: Yes: circuit breakers, admission control, and upstream rate limits. During failover we can cap traffic to the secondary and use autoscaling triggers, but autoscaling has warmup times so canaries are safer.
00:03:10 Samir: Would Redwood route to third-party providers as a last resort? We sometimes use external LLM providers.
00:03:15 Maya: There's an option to plug external endpoints as fallbacks. It can work but adds policy complexity and different SLAs. Some customers use it as a final failover.
00:03:25 Renee: Telemetry requirements: per-request token count, p50/p95/p99, model version, region, and cache hit metrics.
00:03:33 Priya: All available via Console and exportable to Prometheus/Grafana; logs can be pushed to S3 or a SIEM. We'll include example dashboards.
00:03:42 Alex: Acceptance criteria?
00:03:45 Maya: Proposal: (1) 2-week pilot with a targeted 50 RPS smoke test, (2) a chaos test simulating primary region degradation, (3) security/compliance sign-off.
00:03:55 Samir: If pilot shows <350ms p95 during failover and no jurisdiction breaches, we'll look at a dedicated pilot commit.
00:04:02 Renee: Ensure rollback steps and playbook ownership are clear.
00:04:06 Diego: We'll include rollback and alert thresholds in the runbook.
00:04:11 Alex: Commercially we need a clear cost delta for failover scenarios.
00:04:15 Maya: We'll send a cost matrix: hosted baseline, reserved capacity, dedicated reserve for secondaries, and private TCO, annotated with expected failover deltas.
00:04:24 Lena: Please include SOC2 and recent pen-test summary in the security pack.
00:04:29 Priya: Will do.
00:04:34 Alex: Timeline: Nova to provide traffic profile and regulatory constraints by 2027-10-06; Redwood to deliver playbook and pricing by 2027-10-05; plan smoke test week of 2027-10-11.
00:04:44 Maya: Closing recap: we'll follow up with docs and a pilot calendar invite. Thanks all.

[Call ends]

Transcription notes: medium quality, occasional speaker label shifts and minor transcription errors for acronyms (e.g., Q8, KV cache).
